title: Always Prioritise Your Health, Then Your Team’s
author: Dominic Salles
summary: This is Chapter 6 of Dominic Salles's The Head of Department Manifesto, serialised on his Substack, and it opens by arguing that a middle leader must protect their own physical and mental health before looking after a team. He uses his own history as a strongman and rowing competitor to show how well-meant routines can damage a body, and argues that most mental health difficulties short of clinical conditions respond to exercise, diet, sleep and a change of perspective. The chapter then turns to the anxieties of a head of department, such as what colleagues think and what happens if results fall, and recommends focusing on impact and on what is within one's control. It offers a four-step Not So Difficult Conversation Checklist built on presenting data, asking for causes, finding evidence and agreeing solutions. The rest applies the Pareto Principle to the few tasks that drive most impact and supplies checklists for common disruptions and for Ofsted preparation.
points: A head of department should treat their own health as the first responsibility, because neglect compounds with age and undermines everything they do for the team.
Most day-to-day anxieties about colleagues' opinions and exam results concern things outside the leader's control, so effort should go to measuring and spreading impact on learning.
The Not So Difficult Conversation Checklist of data, causes, evidence and solutions turns awkward performance discussions into collaborative problem solving.
Teachers are more persuaded by data they gather themselves, as in the example of a teacher choosing to time a Do Now that was running long.
The Pareto Principle tells a middle leader to identify the small share of tasks, such as coaching and curriculum, that produce most of the impact.
quotes: Warren Buffet likens your body to a car. Imagine being given a car on your 17th birthday, but knowing that this would be the only car you could ever own.
My point is not that age is going to mess up your best laid plans – you know that already – it is that if you don’t pay attention to your health, you are going to be way more screwed than I am.
I don’t mean this in any way to dismiss mental health issues – I am simply saying that most of the solutions are entirely within your control.
Measure the impact on learning of everything you and your team do. Celebrate what is working, and find ways to spread it.
Do you know any teacher or head of department who has been sacked because exam results went down? No, you don’t. This is an illogical fear – nothing will happen except your reaction.
There is no such thing as a difficult conversation – you have just made it difficult by characterising it this way.
Remember, the data teachers gather for themselves is far more persuasive than the data you gather. Next time you visit, it is easy to spot if the timer is on and set to a reasonable limit.
The Pareto Principle tells us that 80% of the things we do have minimal impact. Instead, 80% of our impact happens because of the 20% of things we do.
